details:
**The Incoherence of the Incoherence (Tahafut al-Tahafut)**
Averroes's most famous work, a point-by-point defense of philosophy against al-Ghazali's attack in The Incoherence of the Philosophers. Its title answers Ghazali's directly, and it is the most common title clue and giveaway for him.

**Commentaries on Aristotle**
Averroes wrote short, middle, and long commentaries on nearly all of Aristotle's works, reviving the careful study of Aristotle. They were so influential in Latin Europe that medieval scholastics simply called him "The Commentator," just as Aristotle was "The Philosopher."

**Refuting Neoplatonist readings of Aristotle**
Averroes tried to recover the "pure" Aristotle by removing the Neoplatonic elements that earlier Muslim philosophers, especially Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and al-Farabi, had blended into Aristotelian thought.

**"Double truth"**
A doctrine linked to Averroes's Latin followers, the "Latin Averroists" such as Siger of Brabant, holding that something can be true in philosophy while its opposite is true in theology. Averroes himself argued that philosophy and religion agree, so the doctrine is usually credited to his heirs rather than to him.

**Rejection of the wahm (estimative faculty)**
In his theory of memory, Averroes describes a process of "spiritualization" in which perceptions are progressively stripped of their matter. The theory resembles Avicenna's account of the internal senses, but Averroes rejects Avicenna's distinct estimative faculty, the wahm, which was supposed to grasp non-sensory meanings such as a sheep sensing a wolf's hostility.

**God as simple, changeless, and the source of plurality**
Averroes held that God is perfectly simple and unchanging, yet can be the cause of a complex, plural world. He explained this by God's single, timeless act of knowing all of reality at once, rather than by a series of separate acts that would introduce change into God.

**Ibn Rushd of Córdoba**
Averroes is the Latinized name of Abu al-Walid Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a 12th-century philosopher born in Córdoba in Muslim Spain (al-Andalus). He also served as a qadi (Islamic judge) and as court physician to the Almohad caliphs.

**The Decisive Treatise (Fasl al-Maqal)**
A legal-philosophical work arguing that Islamic law actually commands the study of philosophy for those capable of it. It holds that true philosophy and true revelation cannot conflict, and that apparent conflicts should be resolved by interpreting scripture allegorically.

**Unity of the intellect (monopsychism)**
Averroes's reading of Aristotle's De Anima, holding that there is a single material (possible) intellect shared by all humans. Thomas Aquinas attacked this view in On the Unity of the Intellect against the Averroists, since it seemed to rule out personal immortality.

**Condemnations of 1270 and 1277**
The Bishop of Paris, Étienne Tempier, condemned lists of propositions associated with the Latin Averroists, including the eternity of the world and the unity of the intellect. These condemnations show how controversial Averroes's influence was at the University of Paris.

**Kitab al-Kulliyat (Colliget)**
Averroes's encyclopedia of medicine, known in Latin as the Colliget. It reflects his career as a physician alongside his philosophical and legal work.

**Appearances in Dante and Raphael**
In the Inferno, Dante places Averroes in Limbo among the virtuous non-Christians, describing him as the one "who made the great commentary." Averroes is also traditionally identified as a turbaned figure in Raphael's fresco The School of Athens.
